newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China, HK, Taiwan markets recover from Deng news.
newsitem.headline: China, HK, Taiwan markets recover from Deng news.

text.p: Stocks in China, Hong Kong and Taiwan closed mostly higher on Thursday on renewed positive sentiment after the death of China's paramount leader, Deng Xiaoping, removed recent uncertainties from the markets.
Hong Kong stocks had jumped 2.33 percent by the close, or 305.01 points, after an initial loss of 92 points.
"I think what you've seen today is really a typical sell the rumour, buy the news," said Richard Verin, head of equities trading at CS First Boston in Hong Kong.
"Investors feel that the last detectable uncertainty in China has been removed with the death of Deng Xiaoping," said Peter So, deputy head of research at Schroder Securities.

Reaction in U.S. markets had been muted, with the Dow Jones industrial average shedding 47.33 points to 7,020.13. Many other Asian markets also showed little response to the news, focusing instead on domestic considerations.
Tokyo shares soared nearly 500 points on investor enthusiasm over a Japanese newspaper report that the government may use public funds to help clear problem loans at the country's banks.
China's B share indices ended mixed, with Shanghai shares ending lower on overseas selling after recovering from early sharp losses.
The Shanghai foreign-currency B share index ended down 0.455 points, or 0.7 percent, lower at 64.675, while Shenzhen's B shares were up 1.26 percent, or 1.78 points, at 143.53.
"Deng's death is without a doubt the most important market factor today," one trader said.
Another trader added: "Today's market performance was much better than expected but trading should be more volatile due to concerns about stability."
In Taiwan, the government moved swiftly to foster stability in its market following Deng's death.
The central bank said it would inject funds into the banking system to ensure sufficient liquidity and a government spokesman said it was prepared to support financial markets.
The weighted index rebounded from an earlier fall to close 21.19 points, or 0.28 percent higher at 7,678.04.

Thai stocks powered ahead as bargain hunters went after inexpensive blue-chip stocks. Traders said they had already discounted the news of Deng's death because there had been so many recent rumours concerning his health.
The SET index closed 15.96 points, or 2.18 percent, higher at 747.70.
Traders said Malaysian stocks were unfazed by Deng's death and blue chips ended higher.
The Composite Index ended up 7.58 points, or 0.60 percent, at 1,266.22.
Singapore stocks rebounded from morning lows and were higher in late trading, but off the highs of the day. The Straits Times index ended up 4.99 points, or 0.22 percent, at 2,251.98.
Australian shares mirrored Wall Street, ending lower on profit-taking. Deng's death was not a market factor.
The All Ordinaries share index was off 14.7 points, or 0.59 percent at 2,476.30.
Similarly, New Zealand stocks ended off their lows, with Deng's death having no impact. The market finished down 3.50 points, or 0.15 percent, at 2,325.85.

Deng's death had little impact on the foreign exchange market, although the U.S. dollar did weaken against the yen on speculative selling. The U.S. currency was quoted at 123.90 yen in late Tokyo trade, after tounching a high of 124.62.
"As far as the foreign exchange market is concerned, Deng's been dead for two or three years anyway," one trader said.
Gold markets in Asia also shrugged off the news of Deng's death, while London Metal Exchange prices barely moved during Asian trading hours.
Gold was quoted at $344.70/345.00 per ounce at the Tokyo close, against $345.00/345.50 in New York on Wednesday.
